doc.title: Mat Domber interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Meeting Rick Fay and making the first recording; Dan Barrett
summary: Domber meets Rick Fay in Orlando, records him in 1989, then Dan Barrett, and the label grows by happenstance.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: and Muggsy Spanier. I mean those were the people that I grew up with as a listener. And I was always a jazz fan. All my life I collected records and that sort of thing. And then I met up with a musician by the name of Rick Fay. Rick was playing in California and I used to go out to California on business and we got to be friends and we discovered that we had a lot of musical tastes in common. And then when they opened the — and he played at the Disney park in Anaheim — and then when they opened the park in Orlando they asked him to come over from California to lead one of the bands. And we’d moved down to Florida. I got involved in business in Florida and I came down and one day he called me and he said “hey you’ve got to come up here and hear this group that I’ve got, really a hot group.” So I did, and that was Rick Fay’s Hot Five that was playing at a little bar, the Cork Room in Orlando, Florida. And after the performance I said to Rick, “Gee this group really sounds good, I’d like to get some of your records.” And Rick said, “I’ve never recorded.” I said, “You’ve been in the business for 40 years and you’ve never recorded? Would you like to?” And that really, in 1989, was our first recording session. It came out in 1990. And that sort of changed me from just a fan to maybe a participant in the business of music. And then one thing led to another. I mean one musician introduced me to another, I broadened my listening interests from strictly Pee Wee Russell and Muggsy Spanier and Eddie Condon and Wild Bill Davison you know, and all of that stuff, and traveled around with Rick to various festivals where he started to perform. I got to know some musicians. We met Dan Barrett. Dan had played with Rick when he was about 16 years old in California. And one day Rick called me and said you know Dan had a very nice music career and was building a following at Concord but they were no longer interested. For some reason or other Carl Jefferson didn’t like trombones I understand. But in any event they dropped Dan as one of their contract artists. So Rick said to me, “Gee it would be nice to do a record with Dan Barrett.” Because I discovered that in order to get publicity, in order to get circulation for a record you couldn’t just have one. No distributor wanted to handle your product if you had one CD. They want a continuing flow of business and a continuing flow of music. So I decided well I was very fortunate that we got a couple of reviews of Rick Fay’s music in Jazz Times and other places, but there was no follow-up. So I said yeah, let’s do the record with Dan Barrett. So we did and through Dan, Dan became our music director for a while, and through him I got to meet people like Howard Alden and Ken Peplowski and people that were part of his circle. And gradually things expanded. And everything happened by happenstance. I mean I never really set out to build —
You never had a big business plan and here’s how we’re going to do this.
